full_judgment:
M.H. Rahman, J: This application under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been filed by defendants Nos. 1 and 2, the TSS PACIFIC ABETO and her owner. It has been contended that on the facts disclosed in the plaint this court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and that the alleged cause of action does not come within the scope of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. 

 6. In 1891 the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the High Court in England-was exercised under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 of the British Parliament. The High Court Division of this Court exercises the same jurisdiction in view of section 2(2) of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890. 

 7. The plaintiffs have relied on section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, which reads as follows: 

 9. Finding it difficult to bring the plaintiffs' case with any of the provisions of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs has invoked the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 of England and has relied on section 1(1). (h) of that Act which gives jurisdiction to the High Court of England to hear and determine any claim arising out of any agreement to the carriage of goods in a ship or the use or hire of a ship. In support of his contention that the Administration of Justice Act of 1956 Of England is applicable to this Court the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs has cited Al-Sayer Navigation Co. V. Delta International Traders Ltd. and Ors. 34 DLR(AD) 110, and drawn my attention to paragraphs 9 to 11 of the report where the, charges in the Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court of England were noted. 

 11. In National Co. Ltd. V. Asia Mariner 72 C.W.N. 635; decided in 1967; it was held that the British Statutes subsequent to 1861 by which the Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court in England was extended or affected were not applicable to India. The same view was held in Mrs. Sahida Ismail V. Petko R. Salvejkov, and Ors. AIR 1973 Bombay 18. 

 12. In Al-Sayer Navigation Co. V. Delta International Traders Ltd. and ors. 34 DLR. (AD) 110, their Lordships of the Appellate Division noted that the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the Court of England was enlarged and "there has been a sea-change in the law since 1861." It was, however not laid down in the decision that the "sea-change" has also affected the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court. 

 13. In view of the clear provisions of sub-section 2 of section 2 of the Act of 180 and the judicial decisions referred to above, I hold that the Admiralty Act of 1861 still holds the field and the Administration of Justice Act of 1956 of England is not applicable in Bangladesh.
